title: The Analog Delusion.
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Nick Potkalitsky responds to Jared Cooney Horvath's The Digital Delusion not by refuting its research but by examining what makes it persuasive and why simple refutation won't work. Horvath's book is simultaneously a research synthesis and an activist manual, and its rhetorical power lies in how smoothly it moves between them — initial propositions that appear fair gradually give way to sweeping conclusions. The 'analog delusion' of Potkalitsky's title is the belief that removing technology from classrooms returns students to authentic, deep learning; in reality it returns to a past that was neither as effective nor as equitable as remembered. A genuine response to Horvath must hold two things at once: legitimate concerns about technology misuse, and evidence that pedagogy-led technology integration can extend what students learn.
points: Horvath's Digital Delusion functions simultaneously as research synthesis and activist manual, with templates for petitions, tech-free manifestos, and parent coalition letters.
The rhetorical danger is in Horvath's long lists of propositions: they begin with widely-accepted claims and slide toward far more contested conclusions.
The 'analog delusion' is the belief that removing technology from classrooms restores authentic learning — it restores a past that was neither as effective nor as equitable as remembered.
Simple refutation of Horvath's research claims will not move the needle on techlash; a holistic and persuasive alternative vision is needed.
A genuine response must hold legitimate concerns about technology misuse alongside evidence that pedagogy-led technology integration genuinely extends student learning.
quotes: I don't think such critique will move the needle of techlash. I think we need a holistic and persuasive alternative to Horvath's deconstructive vision.
Research seamlessly gives way to invective. Personal stories, narrative, and metaphor breathe life into evidence and statistics.

His characterization of the 'Ideology of AI' begins with the tenet that 'Human Thought Is Best Represented in Language' — but by the final item, AI enthusiasts believe 'Only AI Can Find the Hidden Patterns of Human Thought.' How far we have travelled from the initial starting point!
The 'analog delusion' is the belief that removing technology from classrooms returns us to some prelapsarian state of authentic, deep learning. It does not.

A response to Horvath must hold two things at once: the legitimate concerns about tech's misuse in schools, and the evidence that thoughtful technology integration — when pedagogy leads — can genuinely extend what students learn and become.
